attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his reply to Booch on his own Substack.

semantics.note: Firm 'will', no deadline. 'Gradually' fairly reflects 'just get more and more' and the context of no single magic day.

contract.note: Plain reading of a continuing trend in dependability and breadth is ordinary. It rightly says a finite period cannot settle an undated, continuing trend.

evidence.note: 2026 AI Index: benchmark gains across domains in 2025, but agents still fail about one in three attempts. This fits the direction of the forecast but cannot settle an open-ended trend.
METR: time horizon on software tasks doubling about every seven months, attributed partly to greater reliability. The task domain is narrow, and it is a finite period.
Nature 2024: scaled-up models give plausible but wrong answers more often. This is a caution about particular model families, not a lasting reversal.

reviews.rationale: This is an undated forecast of a continuing trend. The evidence points the same way (broader benchmark gains, longer task horizons), and the reliability caveats in e3 are not a lasting reversal. But the contract says no finite period of improvement can settle the forecast, and no conclusive event has happened. So it stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words on his own Substack.

semantics.note: 'I don't think we will waste more than 5 years' is an ordinary statement of belief, not a probability hedge, so it is scorable. The five-year horizon and 'substantial fraction' are kept. The streetlight is LLM-centred work, according to the context.

contract.note: The deadline of 2028-01-22, counted from publication, is fair. 'Substantial fraction' and 'AI effort' have no measure, and the boundary for hybrid work is unclear. The contract admits the result depends on how these are read.

evidence.note: Meta's own announcement of the V-JEPA 2 world model is one example of non-LLM work. It gives no field-wide denominator, so it cannot show a substantial share.

reviews.rationale: The deadline is 2028-01-22, after the evaluation date. The early-resolution rule needs representative field-wide records of a substantial share, and the packet has only one company project. So the claim is not due and unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words on his own Substack.

semantics.note: This states an architectural requirement for achieving AGI. 'I think ... no choice' is a firm belief. It could also be read as conditional on AGI being reached, and that antecedent is unmet either way.

contract.note: It treats the claim as a necessity claim and requires a verified AGI with disclosed architecture to settle it. That is demanding but fair to 'no choice'.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own release claims GPT-6 Astra saturates several benchmarks. It does not establish AGI under the context's standard and discloses no architecture.
DeepMind evaluation framework and hackathon. It is a way of measuring, not evidence about which architectures AGI needs.
Outside evaluation finds Astra has embodied competence but not yet practical embodied intelligence. That suggests the AGI standard is not met, and it says nothing about necessity.

reviews.rationale: No independently verified AGI with disclosed architecture appears in the packet. Nothing shows either that the hybrid approach is necessary or that a system without it reached AGI. The forecast has no deadline and no conclusive event, so it is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words on his own Substack.

semantics.note: Revision 2 keeps the scope words 'a decent fraction' and 'many', and 'some expected'. It is a claim about how widely two beliefs were held in the community.

contract.note: The evaluator chose the reporting window, 2022 to the publication date, which is reasonable. Reading 'decent fraction' and 'many' as a sizeable minority is fair, and so is the plain reading of 'bullshit'.

evidence.note: 2022 NLP survey: 51% agreed LMs understand language. This shows broad scepticism among NLP researchers. It does not measure the 'primary forte' belief, and the population is narrower than the AI community.

Ford's own disclosure that Level 4 autonomy is further out than anticipated and that it took an impairment on Argo. This is one company's reassessment, not a measure of how common the belief was in the AI community.

reviews.rationale: The contract needs evidence of how widely each belief was held. The packet has related scepticism in NLP and one carmaker's retreat on autonomy, but no measure of either specific belief across the AI community. Nothing shows either belief was fringe. Unresolved.
